Flooding Disrupts Operations at Guernsey Hospitality Sites as Storm Persists

Severe flooding caused by ongoing heavy rains is impacting hospitality operations across Guernsey, with multiple hotels, guesthouses, and leisure premises reporting significant disruptions and damage as of Friday. The situation remains critical as the storm continues, hampering cleanup and recovery efforts at affected sites.

Hospitality Guernsey, the island’s trade association, said in a statement that at least 15 member properties have reported partial or full closure due to water ingress, flooding of basement facilities, or impassable access routes within their premises. “We are seeing unprecedented water levels at several sites, with ground-floor guest rooms, kitchens, and staff areas inundated,” said spokesperson Marie Vaudin. “Many employees have been unable to report to work, and those on shift have faced difficult conditions.”

At the Harbour View Hotel in St. Peter Port, management confirmed that the ground-level dining area and conference rooms have been rendered unusable. “We’ve had to move all guests to upper floors and suspend dining services,” said general manager Colin Le Page. “Our staff are working tirelessly, but the water is still rising in some parts of the building.”

Several smaller guesthouses along the coast have also reported significant property damage, particularly to communal lounges, staff accommodation, and on-site leisure facilities. “Our team is focused on keeping everyone safe and dry, but we’ve had to cancel all bookings for the foreseeable future,” said a representative of Seabreeze Inn.

The Hospitality Workers’ Union has expressed concern for employees affected by the ongoing closures and hazardous conditions. “Many of our members are unable to work or are stranded at their workplaces,” said union secretary Jeanette Ferbrache. “We are urging employers to prioritize staff safety and support.”

With the storm system predicted to persist over the weekend, operators and staff are bracing for further disruption as floodwaters continue to rise.
